ety.text: From opportune + -ity, from Middle French opportunité, from Latin opportūnitās.

senses.d: A chance for advancement, progress or profit.
ex: seize the opportunity
take an opportunity

senses.d: A favorable circumstance or occasion.
ex: Having a holiday is a great opportunity to relax.

senses.d: Opportuneness.
ex: The Court questioned the opportunity of introducing these measures in such an uncertain economic climate.

grp.label: chance for advancement, progress or profit

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin occāsiōnem (accusative of occāsiō). Compare the inherited Old French ochoison, achaison (the latter being influenced by Latin accūsātiō).
Borrowed from Latin opportūnitātem. Morphologically, from opportun + -ité.
Borrowed from Latin occāsiōnem, whence also Italian cagione (an inherited doublet).

pt:oportunidade.gl: opportunity (chance for advancement, progress or profit)

From Middle English opposicioun, from Old French oposicion (whence French opposition), from Late Latin oppositiō, translating Ancient Greek ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis), from the past participle stem of classical Latin oppōnō (“to set against”). Equivalent to oppose + -ition.

senses.d: The action of opposing or of being in conflict.
ex: The two politicians are in opposition to the bill.
The proposal met with strong opposition from local residents.

senses.d: An opposite or contrasting position.
ex: Near-synonym: oppositeness
These ideas are in opposition to each other.

senses.d: The apparent relative position of two celestial bodies when one is at an angle of 180 degrees from the other as seen from the Earth.
A political party or movement opposed to the party or government in power.
ex: leader of the opposition

senses.d: In United States intellectual property law, a proceeding in which an interested party seeks to prevent the registration of a trademark or patent.
A position in which the player on the move must yield with his king allowing his opponent to advance with his own king.
The difference of quantity or quality between two propositions having the same subject and predicate.

grp.label: action of opposing; being in conflict
politics: party or movement opposed to government

From Middle English opposen, from Old French opposer, from Latin ob (“before, against”) + Medieval Latin pono (“to put”), taking the place of Latin opponere (“to oppose”).

senses.d: To attempt to stop the progression of; to resist or antagonize by physical means, or by arguments, etc.; to contend against.
ex: to oppose the king in battle
to oppose a bill in Congress

senses.d: To object to.
ex: Many religious leaders oppose cloning humans.

senses.d: To present or set up in opposition; to pose.
ex: They are opposed to any form of hierarchy.

, Book I
I may […] oppose my single opinion to his.

senses.d: To place in front of, or over against; to set opposite; to exhibit.
ex: Her grace sat down […] / In a rich chair of state; opposing freely / The beauty of her person to the people.

grp.label: to attempt to stop the progression of; to resist or antagonize by physical means, or by arguments, etc.
to present or set up in opposition; to pose
to place in front of, or over against; to set opposite; to exhibit

it:opporre.gl: to put forward, raise (points of view, arguments)

es:oponer.gl: to pit (one thing against another); to set in opposition

ety.text: Likely a semi-learned borrowing from Latin oppōnere, modified by analogy with inherited pôr.
From Latin obiectum (“object”, literally “thrown against”), from obiectus, perfect passive participle of obiciō (“throw against”), from ob (“against”) + iaciō (“throw”).

chain.g: to hold forth, present, show, exhibit, display, reveal

ety.text: Inherited from Middle English opposit, borrowed from Old French oposite, from Latin oppositus, perfect passive participle of oppōnō (“to oppose”). Compare oppose.

senses.d: Located directly across from something else, or from each other.
ex: She saw him walking on the opposite side of the road.

senses.d: Of leaves and flowers, positioned directly across from each other on a stem.
Facing in the other direction.
ex: They were moving in opposite directions.

senses.d: Of either of two complementary or mutually exclusive things.
ex: He is attracted to the opposite sex.

senses.d: Extremely different; inconsistent; contrary; antagonistic.
ex:
, Book III
Particles of speech have divers, and sometimes almost opposite, significations.
Novels, by which the reader is misled into another sort of pieasure opposite to that which is designed in an epick poem.

senses.d: A person or thing that is importantly (substantively) different from someone or something else.
Especially, one that is different to the extreme degree of being the reverse.
An opponent.
ex: The dogfighter fought closely with his opposite.

senses.d: A counterpart.
ex: The Swedish diplomat worked closely with his opposite from Denmark.

senses.d: An antonym.
ex: "Up" is the opposite of "down".

senses.d: An additive inverse.
In an opposite position.
ex: I was on my seat and she stood opposite.
Where's the bus station? -Over there, just opposite.

senses.d: On another channel at the same time.
Facing, or across from.
ex: There’s a bus stop opposite the faculty entrance, right on the other side of the road.

senses.d: In a complementary role to.
ex: He played opposite Marilyn Monroe.

senses.d: On another channel at the same time.
ex: The game show Just Men! aired opposite The Young and the Restless on CBS.

chain.g: to turn upside-down, over or around, invert, upset

phr: on opposite sides of the barricades

senses.d: That opposes or oppose; on the opposite side.
ex: opposing armies
opposing players

ety.text: From Middle English oppression, from Old French oppression, from Latin oppressiō (“a pressing down, violence, oppression”), from opprimō; see oppress.

senses.d: The exercise of authority or power in a burdensome, cruel, or unjust manner.
The act of oppressing, or the state of being oppressed.
ex: Extreme freedom is followed by extreme oppression, said Plato.

senses.d: A feeling of being oppressed. Special usage may include a sense of heaviness or obstruction in the body or mind; depression; dullness; lassitude.
ex: Our oppression was lifted by the reappearance of the sun.

grp.label: exercise of authority or power in a burdensome, cruel, or unjust manner
act of oppressing, or the state of being oppressed

senses.d: Subject to oppression.
ex: politically oppressed
feel oppressed

senses.d: Acting in opposition; opposing.
Being, of having an opponent; not unopposed.
Opposite.
ex: The diagonally opposed driving positions in the cab are identical.

grp.label: being, of having an opponent; not unopposed

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin oppōnēns (“opposing”), present active participle of oppōnō (“to oppose”).

senses.d: One who opposes another; one who works or takes a position against someone or something; one who attempts to stop the progress of someone or something.
ex: The person who ran against her in the last election proved to be a formidable opponent.
During the crackdown, many opponents of the regime were arrested.

senses.d: One who opposes another physically (in a fight, sport, game, or competition).
ex: […] it is possible for a good [draughts] player to defeat an opponent without capturing his pieces.

senses.d: One who opposes another in words (in a dispute, argument or controversy).
ex: It is easier to confound than to convince an opponent; the former may be effected by a turn that has more happiness than truth in it.

senses.d: One who is opposed or objects (to a policy, course of action or set of ideas).
ex: She was a dedicated opponent of the death penalty.
Their Oath is to maintain the Romish-Catholick Religion, and persecute all Opponents to it.

senses.d: The participant who opens an academic debate by putting forward objections to a theological or philosophical thesis.
Opposing; adverse; antagonistic.
Situated in front; opposite.
ex:
Her sympathizing Lover takes his Stand
High on th’ opponent Bank […]

grp.label: one who opposes another in words
one who objects to a policy, etc.
